title: Humour and wordplay: Mulla, the cat and the pun
intro: Iranians are great tellers of jokes, and they have been laughing in Persian for a very long time: at Mulla Nasreddin's crooked logic, at Obeyd Zakani's hypocritical cat, at puns that only work in Persian. In this lesson you read two classic comic tales, learn the words for joking, teasing and satire – and the difference between a friendly tease and a rude remark – see how Persian puns (جناس) work, and practise telling a joke the way Iranians tell it.
goals: read and retell a Mulla Nasreddin anecdote and Obeyd Zakani's tale of the mouse and the cat
tell a friendly tease (سر به سر گذاشتن، شوخی کردن) from mockery and rude remarks (مسخره کردن، متلک انداختن)
recognise puns built on Persian homonyms such as شیر، سیر، باز and گور
tell a short joke in the storytelling present: یک روز ملا می‌رود…

sections.title: The pot that had a baby
sections.intro: Mulla Nasreddin – usually just 'the Mulla' – is the wise fool of a thousand stories told from the Balkans to Central Asia. Here is one of the best known, retold in plain written Persian.

sections.title: How Iranians joke
sections.md:
Persian humour has a few favourite moves:

- **Crooked logic.** The Mulla never lies outright; he takes an idea seriously until it turns absurd – a pot that gives birth must be able to die.
- **The quick retort.** Iranians admire [[حاضرجوابی|hāzer-javābi|quick-wittedness]], the answer that turns the tables in one line.
- **Wordplay.** Persian is full of words that look or sound alike, and poets have played with them for a thousand years. The rhetorical term is [[جناس|jenās]].
- **Satire.** From Obeyd Zakani in the fourteenth century to today's newspapers and social media, [[طنز|tanz]] has been a safe-ish way to criticise the powerful – a cat can say what a person cannot.
- **Teasing among friends.** [[سر به سر گذاشتن|sar be sar gozāshtan]] is a sign of closeness: you tease people you like.

Jokes travel fast in Iran – by text message, in shared taxis, at family gatherings. Like everywhere, some joke cycles target particular towns or peoples. This course leaves them out, and it is wise to do the same: they are the quickest way to stop people laughing *with* you.

Finally, Iranians laugh a great deal at themselves – at ta'ārof, at traffic, at the Persian love of long titles. Self-mockery is often the friendliest humour of all.

ex.en: I was joking – don't be upset!

sections.title: Joking, teasing, mocking: knowing the difference
sections.md:
Persian draws clear lines between kinds of laughter, and the verbs tell you which side of the line you are on. [[شوخی کردن|shukhi kardan]] and [[سر به سر کسی گذاشتن|sar be sar-e kas-i gozāshtan]] are friendly: they assume you are close. [[دست انداختن|dast andākhtan]] is playful but can sting. [[مسخره کردن|maskhare kardan]] is unkind, and [[متلک انداختن|matalak andākhtan]] – a snide remark, or a remark shouted at a stranger in the street – is plain rude.

If a tease has gone too far, repair it at once: [[شوخی کردم!|shukhi kardam!|I was only joking!]], [[به دل نگیر|be del na-gir|don't take it to heart]].

sections.title: Puns: جناس
sections.md:
A Persian pun usually rests on one of two things:

1. **One word, two meanings** – the same spelling and sound: [[شیر|shir]] is a lion, milk and a tap; [[سیر|sir]] is garlic and 'full after eating'. Rhetoric calls this *jenās-e tām*, the complete pun.
2. **Two words that differ by one vowel or letter** – since short vowels are not written, they even *look* the same: [[کشتی|kashti|ship]] and [[کشتی|koshti|wrestling]], [[نه|na|no]] and [[نه|noh|nine]].

Poets used both constantly. A famous quatrain attributed to Khayyam ends on the two meanings of [[گور|gur]] – the wild ass that King Bahram loved to hunt (he was nicknamed Bahram-e Gur), and the grave:

> [[بهرام که گور می‌گرفتی همه عمر / دیدی که چگونه گور بهرام گرفت؟|bahrām ke gur mi-gerefti hame 'omr / didi ke chegune gur bahrām gereft?|Bahram, you who caught wild asses all your life – did you see how the grave caught Bahram?]]

Puns are the jokes that translate worst. When an Iranian groans [[بی‌مزه!|bi-maze!|lame!]] at your first Persian pun, take it as a compliment.

sections.title: Telling a joke the Iranian way
sections.md:
When Iranians tell a joke or an anecdote aloud, they switch into the **storytelling present**: [[یک روز ملا می‌رود بازار|yek ruz Mollā mi-ravad bāzār|one day the Mulla goes to the market]] – just as English says *so this guy walks into a bar*. Speech is quoted with [[می‌گوید|mi-guyad]] (spoken *mi-ge*) and no 'that'. Characters are often just [[طرف|taraf|the guy]] or [[یارو|yāru|this fellow]] – but یارو sounds rude about a real person, so keep it for jokes.

The punchline comes last and stands alone, often after a pause or a [[خلاصه|kholāse|anyway]]. Here is another famous Mulla story told that way – the written form first, then the way you would hear it at a dinner table.

sections.title: Obeyd Zakani: the mouse and the cat
sections.intro: Obeyd Zakani (died about 1370) lived in Shiraz in the age of Hafez and was the sharpest satirist of classical Persian. His *Mouse and Cat* is a short comic epic in verse; it starts its story with the line [[از قضای فلک یکی گربه / بود چون اژدها به کرمانا|az ghazā-ye falak yek-i gorbe / bud chon ezhdehā be Kermānā|by the will of heaven there was a cat in Kerman, like a dragon]]. Here it is retold in modern prose.

sentences.fa: عبید زاکانی، شاعر و طنزنویس قرن هشتم هجری، داستان موش و گربه را به شعر سروده است.
sentences.r: Obeyd Zākāni, shā'er o tanz-nevis-e gharn-e hashtom-e hejri, dāstān-e mush o gorbe rā be she'r sorude ast.
sentences.en: Obeyd Zakani, poet and satirist of the eighth century of the Hijra – the fourteenth century AD – told the story of the mouse and the cat in verse.
sentences.faV: عُبَید زاکانی، شاعِر و طَنزنِویسِ قَرنِ هَشتُمِ هِجری، داستانِ موش و گُربه را به شِعر سُروده اَست.

sentences.fa: در کرمان گربه‌ای بود به بزرگی اژدها که همه از او می‌ترسیدند.
sentences.r: dar Kermān gorbe-i bud be bozorgi-ye ezhdehā ke hame az u mi-tarsidand.
sentences.en: In Kerman there was a cat as big as a dragon, and everyone was afraid of him.
sentences.faV: دَر کِرمان گُربه‌ای بود به بُزُرگیِ اِژدِها که هَمه اَز او می‌تَرسیدَند.

sentences.fa: روزی گربه به شرابخانه رفت تا موش شکار کند.
sentences.r: ruz-i gorbe be sharāb-khāne raft tā mush shekār konad.
sentences.en: One day the cat went into a wine cellar to hunt mice.
sentences.faV: روزی گُربه به شَرابخانه رَفت تا موش شِکار کُنَد.

sentences.fa: موشی از خم شراب خورده بود و مست شده بود.
sentences.r: mush-i az khom-e sharāb khorde bud o mast shode bud.
sentences.en: A mouse had drunk from a wine jar and was drunk.
sentences.faV: موشی اَز خُمِ شَراب خورده بود و مَست شُده بود.

sentences.fa: موش مست فریاد می‌زد: «گربه کجاست تا سرش را بکنم؟»
sentences.r: mush-e mast faryād mi-zad: «gorbe kojā-st tā sar-ash rā bekanam?»
sentences.en: The drunken mouse was shouting, 'Where's that cat? I'll tear his head off!'
sentences.faV: موشِ مَست فَریاد می‌زَد: «گُربه کُجاست تا سَرَش را بِکَنَم؟»

sentences.fa: گربه از پشت خم بیرون پرید و موش را گرفت و خورد.
sentences.r: gorbe az posht-e khom birun parid o mush rā gereft o khord.
sentences.en: The cat leapt out from behind the jar, caught the mouse and ate him.
sentences.faV: گُربه اَز پُشتِ خُم بیرون پَرید و موش را گِرِفت و خورد.

sentences.fa: بعد به مسجد رفت، دست و رویش را شست و توبه کرد.
sentences.r: ba'd be masjed raft, dast o ru-yash rā shost o towbe kard.
sentences.en: Then he went to the mosque, washed his hands and face, and repented.
sentences.faV: بَعد به مَسجِد رَفت، دَست و رویَش را شُست و تَوبه کَرد.

sentences.fa: موشی که پشت منبر پنهان شده بود، این خبر را برای موش‌ها برد.
sentences.r: mush-i ke posht-e menbar penhān shode bud, in khabar rā barā-ye mush-hā bord.
sentences.en: A mouse who had been hiding behind the pulpit took the news to the other mice.
sentences.faV: موشی که پُشتِ مِنبَر پِنهان شُده بود، این خَبَر را بَرایِ موش‌ها بُرد.

sentences.fa: موش‌ها خوشحال شدند و هفت موش را با هدیه‌های فراوان پیش گربه فرستادند.
sentences.r: mush-hā khoshhāl shodand o haft mush rā bā hediye-hā-ye farāvān pish-e gorbe ferestādand.
sentences.en: The mice were overjoyed and sent seven mice to the cat with a mountain of presents.
sentences.faV: موش‌ها خوشحال شُدَند و هَفت موش را با هِدیه‌هایِ فَراوان پیشِ گُربه فِرِستادَند.

sentences.fa: هدیه‌ها شراب و کباب و کشمش و خرما و پنیر و برنج بود.
sentences.r: hediye-hā sharāb o kabāb o keshmesh o khormā o panir o berenj bud.
sentences.en: The presents were wine, kebab, raisins, dates, cheese and rice.
sentences.faV: هِدیه‌ها شَراب و کَباب و کِشمِش و خُرما و پَنیر و بِرِنج بود.

sentences.fa: گربه هدیه‌ها را دید و ناگهان پنج موش را با هم گرفت.
sentences.r: gorbe hediye-hā rā did o nāgahān panj mush rā bā ham gereft.
sentences.en: The cat looked at the presents – and suddenly seized five of the mice at once.
sentences.faV: گُربه هِدیه‌ها را دید و ناگَهان پَنج موش را با هَم گِرِفت.

sentences.fa: دو موش فرار کردند و خبر را به پادشاه موش‌ها رساندند.
sentences.r: do mush farār kardand o khabar rā be pādshāh-e mush-hā resāndand.
sentences.en: Two mice escaped and took the news to the king of the mice.
sentences.faV: دو موش فَرار کَردَند و خَبَر را به پادشاهِ موش‌ها رِساندَند.

sentences.fa: پادشاه لشکری بزرگ جمع کرد و گربه در جنگ اسیر شد.
sentences.r: pādshāh lashkar-i bozorg jam' kard o gorbe dar jang asir shod.
sentences.en: The king gathered a great army, and in the battle the cat was taken prisoner.
sentences.faV: پادشاه لَشکَری بُزُرگ جَمع کَرد و گُربه دَر جَنگ اَسیر شُد.

sentences.fa: اما وقتی می‌خواستند او را به دار بزنند، بندها را پاره کرد و لشکر موش‌ها را پراکند.
sentences.r: ammā vaghti mi-khāstand u rā be dār bezanand, band-hā rā pāre kard o lashkar-e mush-hā rā parākand.
sentences.en: But just as they were about to hang him, he broke his bonds and scattered the army of mice.
sentences.faV: اَمّا وَقتی می‌خواستَند او را به دار بِزَنَند، بَندها را پاره کَرد و لَشکَرِ موش‌ها را پَراکَند.

sentences.fa: قرن‌هاست که خوانندگان در این گربه‌ی ریاکار چهره‌ی حاکمان دروغگو را می‌بینند.
sentences.r: gharn-hā-st ke khānandegān dar in gorbe-ye riyākār chehre-ye hākemān-e dorughgu rā mi-binand.
sentences.en: For centuries readers have seen in this hypocritical cat the face of lying rulers.
sentences.faV: قَرن‌هاست که خوانَندِگان دَر این گُربه‌یِ ریاکار چِهره‌یِ حاکِمانِ دُروغگو را می‌بینَند.

sentences.fa: به قول مردم: «توبه‌ی گرگ مرگ است.»
sentences.r: be ghowl-e mardom: «towbe-ye gorg marg ast.»
sentences.en: As people say: 'A wolf's repentance is death' – it only ends when the wolf does.
sentences.faV: به قَولِ مَردُم: «تَوبه‌یِ گُرگ مَرگ اَست.»

options: He boasted loudly that he would kill the cat

questions.q: Why did the mice send presents to the cat?
options: To ask for peace after the war
Because they heard he had repented

sections.title: From Obeyd to the thirteenth of Farvardin
sections.md:
**Obeyd Zakani** wrote in fourteenth-century Shiraz, in the same streets as Hafez, under rulers who alternated between pleasure and harsh piety. Besides *Mouse and Cat* he wrote mock treatises: *The Ethics of the Aristocrats*, which 'proves' that the old virtues are out of date, and a satirical dictionary of *Definitions* in which every respectable title is given a wicked meaning. Many readers see in his pious, murderous cat a portrait of a ruler of his own day; the poem has been read since as a satire on any power that wraps itself in religion.

**Mulla Nasreddin** belongs to everyone. Turks call him Nasreddin Hoca, Central Asians often Afandi, and Arabs tell similar stories of Juha. In Iran his stories are children's books, proverbs and television sketches, and you will hear Iranians quote him without telling the whole story: [[دیگ زایید|dig zāyid]], 'the pot had a baby', is enough.

**The lie of the thirteenth.** On [[سیزده‌بدر|sizdah-bedar]], the thirteenth day of the new year, families picnic outdoors and play tricks on each other. A prank on that day is a [[دروغ سیزده|dorugh-e sizdah|the lie of the thirteenth]] – Iran's April Fool, which some say is older than the European one.

**Why jokes don't translate.** A Persian joke may rest on a pun (شیر، سیر), on an unwritten vowel (کشتی), on the ritual politeness of ta'ārof, on a line of Hafez everybody knows, or on the switch between bookish and street Persian. Explaining it kills it. The surest sign that your Persian has arrived is the day you laugh before the explanation.

sections.title: Tips
items: Laugh at the Mulla, not at people. Jokes about a town, a people or an accent may get a laugh in some company, but they cost friends – leave them alone.
A tease needs a safety net. If your سر به سر گذاشتن lands badly, add at once: [[شوخی کردم، به دل نگیر|shukhi kardam, be del na-gir|I was joking, don't take it to heart]].
Learn a few Mulla stories by heart and tell them in the storytelling present with spoken forms: *ye ruz Mollā mi-re…* It is one of the best fluency exercises there is.
Collect homonyms as you meet them – شیر، سیر، باز، ماه، مهر، شانه. Each one is a pun waiting for you.
In writing, satire is [[طنز|tanz]]; a personal attack in verse is [[هجو|hajv]]. Iranian critics are proud of the first and wary of the second.
If you don't get a joke, say so with a smile: [[نگرفتم!|na-gereftam!|I didn't get it!]] – گرفتن 'to get' works exactly as in English.

items.en: The Mulla said, 'Congratulations! Your pot has had a baby.'
Don't be upset, I was joking!

items.fa: دیگی که زایید، سر زا هم ___.
items.r: dig-i ke zāyid, sar-e zā ham ___.
items.en: A pot that gives birth can also die in childbirth.
I ate garlic and got full.

items.fa: گربه بعد از خوردن موش به مسجد رفت و ___ کرد.
items.r: gorbe ba'd az khordan-e mush be masjed raft o ___ kard.
items.en: After eating the mouse, the cat went to the mosque and repented.

items.fa: این جوک اصلاً خنده‌دار نبود؛ خیلی ___ بود.
items.r: in jok aslan khande-dār na-bud; kheyli ___ bud.
items.en: That joke wasn't funny at all; it was really lame.

items.q: Why does the Mulla say that the pot has died?
options: To keep it, using the neighbour's own logic
Because he forgot where it was
items.explain: If the neighbour accepted that a pot can give birth, he can hardly deny that it can die.

options: making a snide or rude remark
items.explain: متلک is a rude dig or a remark shouted at a stranger – not a friendly tease.
سیر: سیر خوردم و سیر شدم 'I ate garlic and got full'.

items.q: In Obeyd Zakani's poem, the cat stands for…
items.explain: The cat repents in public and goes on killing – the classic hypocrite (ریاکار).

options: a kind of satire on rulers
a play on words that look or sound alike
a funny story about the Mulla
items.explain: جناس is the rhetorical name for a pun, like گور 'grave' and گور 'wild ass' in Khayyam.

items.q: How do Iranians usually tell a joke aloud?
options: in the storytelling present: می‌ره، می‌گه
items.explain: Like English 'so this guy walks into a bar', Persian jokes are told in the present.

items.en: She has a great sense of humour.

items.fa: ملا از همسایه دیگی قرض گرفت.
items.r: Mollā az hamsāye dig-i gharz gereft.
items.en: The Mulla borrowed a pot from the neighbour.
items.faV: مُلّا اَز هَمسایه دیگی قَرض گِرِفت.

items.en: Your pot has had a baby.
I ate garlic and got full.
I was joking – don't be upset!
